title: What are JPA projections and their three forms (interface-based, class-based/DTO with constructor expression, dynamic), and why do they beat loading the full entity?
shortTitle: Interface vs DTO vs dynamic projections?
keyPoints: Interface projection supports SpEL @Value for computed fields like getDisplayName() – a feature DTO projections cannot offer
DTO projection with constructor expression is the fastest: no proxy, no persistence context, direct object creation
Nested interface projections let you project associations (account.getTrades() returns List<TradeView>)
JPQL constructor expressions do not support nested collections – use interface projections for nested data
Dynamic projections accept Class<T> so the same repository method can return different shapes at runtime
For a 20-column entity where the API needs 3 columns, projections reduce data transfer by 85%
Use DTO for production APIs, interface for computed fields and nested projections, full entity only for writes

s1_definition.oneliner: Interface projections support SpEL @Value for computed fields and nested interfaces for associations; DTO projections are the fastest with no proxy overhead; dynamic projections let the caller choose the shape at runtime.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Interface with SpEL** – interface projections support `@Value("#{target.field + ...}")` for computed fields. The SpEL expression evaluates against the target entity at runtime.
- **Nested interface projection** – interfaces can declare nested interfaces for association projections: `List<TradeView> getTrades()`. Spring handles the JOIN and mapping.
- **DTO constructor expression** – `SELECT new Dto(e.f1, e.f2)` creates plain objects directly. No proxy, no persistence context. Does not support nested collections.
- **Dynamic projection** – `<T> List<T> findBy(String x, Class<T> type)` lets the caller pick the return shape. Same method, different projections.
- **Performance** – DTO is fastest (no proxy, no persistence context). Interface adds proxy overhead but enables SpEL and nesting. Full entity is slowest (all columns, snapshots, dirty checking).
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, the full Account entity is like Rajesh's entire 20-page customer file. Interface projection with SpEL is like a pre-printed slip that computes "Rajesh Kumar (SAV2001)" on the fly. Nested interface projection is like a slip that also lists the last 5 trades. DTO projection is like a receipt printed directly from the database with exactly the fields the mobile app needs. Dynamic projection is like Rajesh choosing which slip format he wants at the counter.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Interface projections support two features that DTO projections cannot: SpEL `@Value` for computed fields and nested interface projections for associations. The SpEL expression `#{target.holderName + ' (' + target.accountId + ')'}` computes "Rajesh Kumar (SAV2001)" at runtime without an extra database column. Nested interfaces project both the parent and its collection in one query.

DTO projections are the fastest approach: no proxy, no persistence context, direct object creation. At National Bank of India, Rajesh uses DTO record `TradeOverview(tradeId, symbol, amount)` for the trade listing API – 3 columns instead of 20, 85% less data, 97% less memory. For the account search dropdown, he uses interface projection with SpEL to compute the display name.

Dynamic projections add runtime flexibility: `<T> List<T> findByName(String name, Class<T> type)` lets the mobile API request `AccountSummary.class` (3 fields) while the admin dashboard requests `Account.class` (all fields), both using the same repository method. Always use projections for read-only endpoints. Use full entities only when dirty checking is needed for writes.

Remember one sentence: use DTO projections for production APIs, interface projections for computed fields and nested data, and full entities only for writes.
